blocks.content: Realization is the relationship between an interface and the class that implements it. It's the moment apromise(the interface) gets fulfilled by actual working code (the class).
Understanding realization clearly is the foundation for writing loosely coupled, testable, and extensible Java code.
1. What is Realization?
In OOP and UML, realization is the relationship where a class commits to fulfilling the contract defined by an interface. The interface says what must be done. The class says how it gets done.

ANALOGY: A JOB DESCRIPTION AND AN EMPLOYEE

A job description says: "This role requires the ability to write reports, conduct meetings, and manage budgets." 

It defines the capabilities required but it has no person doing those things yet. When someone gets hired and actually does those things, that's realization. 

The job description is the interface. The employee is the class. The hiring is the implements keyword.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: CreditCardPayment realizes Payable it fulfils the contract with actual code
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781423478490-978203615.png
The Payable interface only declares what every payment method must be able to do: pay() and refund(). It does not contain the actual logic.
CreditCardPayment provides the real implementation of those methods. In other words, it fulfills the contract defined by Payable.
Think of it like this: the interface says "every payment method must know how to pay and refund", and CreditCardPayment says "I know exactly how to do that for credit cards."
The Core Idea: The interface makes a promise. The class keeps it. Realization is the act of keeping that promise providing concrete implementations for every method the interface demands.
2. Interface ( The Contract )
An interface in Java is a pure contract. It declares method signatures what a class must be able to do without providing any implementation of how to do it.
Three things an interface guarantees:

["What: The interface defines the method signatures that every implementing class must provide. It specifies the method name, parameters, and return type, acting as a contract for all classes that realize it.
","Not How: The interface contains no implementation details. It only states what operations must exist. Each class that implements the interface is free to provide its own logic for how those operations are performed.
"]
items: What: The interface defines the method signatures that every implementing class must provide. It specifies the method name, parameters, and return type, acting as a contract for all classes that realize it.

Not How: The interface contains no implementation details. It only states what operations must exist. Each class that implements the interface is free to provide its own logic for how those operations are performed.

blocks.content: ANALOGY: A POWER SOCKET STANDARD
The standard for a Type-B power socket defines: two flat pins at a specific distance, one round ground pin, 120V AC at 60Hz.
Any device that meets this standard can plug in. Any socket that meets it can accept any compliant device.
The standard is the interface it defines what must be supported, not what device will be plugged in or how the electricity is generated.
The power of an interface is that many different classes can realize the same one and any code that depends on the interface works with all of them, without knowing which specific one it's using.
3. Realization in Code
In Java, realization is expressed with the implements keyword. The class must provide a concrete body for every method declared in the interface otherwise the compiler rejects it.
All three classes realize theSortableinterface. They each keep the same promise in completely different ways. Code that usesSortabledoesn't care which one it gets they're all interchangeable.
<u>Understanding:</u>
The Sortable interface defines a contract. It says that every sorting algorithm must provide two methods: one to sort() the data and another to return its name using getName().
The interface only defines what must exist, not how sorting should happen.
Now, QuickSort, MergeSort, and BubbleSort all realize (implement) this interface. That means each class promises to provide its own version of sort() and getName().
The important point is that all three classes follow the same contract, but their internal implementations are completely different.
QuickSort uses the quicksort algorithm, MergeSort uses mergesort, and BubbleSort uses bubblesort.
Because they all implement the same interface, code can work with the Sortable type instead of a specific algorithm.
The caller doesn't need to know whether it's QuickSort or MergeSort. It simply calls sort() and trusts that the object knows how to sort.
Think of it like this:
["Sortable = \"I can sort data\" (promise/contract)","QuickSort = \"I sort using Quick Sort\"","MergeSort = \"I sort using Merge Sort\"","BubbleSort = \"I sort using Bubble Sort\""]
items: Sortable = "I can sort data" (promise/contract)
QuickSort = "I sort using Quick Sort"
MergeSort = "I sort using Merge Sort"
BubbleSort = "I sort using Bubble Sort"

blocks.content: The caller only talks to Sortable, so the sorting algorithm can be swapped anytime without changing the caller's code.
That's the main benefit of realization: same interface, different implementations, all interchangeable.
4. Multiple Interfaces ( One Class )

A class can realize multiple interfaces simultaneously. This is one of the biggest advantages over inheritance Java only allows a class to extend one parent, but it can implement as many interfaces as needed.
Each interface is a separate contract the class is committing to honour.

ANALOGY: A PERSON WITH MULTIPLE ROLES

One person can be a Doctor, a Teacher, and a Volunteer at the same time. Each role defines what they must be able to do in that context. When they're in the hospital, they fulfil the Doctor contract. 

When they're in the classroom, they fulfil the Teacher contract. The person (class) realizes all three roles (interfaces) simultaneously..
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: IMPORTANT OBSERVATION
When a Report is assigned to a Saveable reference, only save() is visible. The other methods are hidden.
This is deliberate it means each part of your system only sees the capabilities relevant to it.
This is called programming to an interface, and it's one of the most powerful tools in OOP.
5. Realization vs Inheritance
These two are easy to confuse both are shown as arrows in UML. The difference is fundamental.
1. Realization (implements)
When a class implements an interface, it is getting a contract only.
Payable says:
"Any class implementing me must provide pay()."
But it gives no code, no data members, and no implementation.
So when CreditCard implements Payable, it must write everything itself.
Interface = RulesClass = Follows those rules
That's realization.
2. Inheritance (extends)
When a class extends another class, it gets actual code and behavior from the parent.
Dog extends Animal
Here, Dog inherits whatever Animal already has, such as:
["name","age","eat()","sleep()"]
items: name
age
eat()
sleep()

blocks.content: So Dog reuses existing code and can add more features of its own.
Parent class = Already built functionalityChild class = Reuses and extends it
1. Relationship

["Realization (implements): A class agrees to follow a set of rules defined by an interface.
","Inheritance (extends): A class reuses and builds upon an existing parent class.
"]
items: Realization (implements): A class agrees to follow a set of rules defined by an interface.
Inheritance (extends): A class reuses and builds upon an existing parent class.

blocks.content: 2. What Does the Child Get?

["Realization: The class gets only the method declarations and must write the implementation itself.
","Inheritance: The child automatically receives fields, methods, and behavior from the parent.
"]
items: Realization: The class gets only the method declarations and must write the implementation itself.
Inheritance: The child automatically receives fields, methods, and behavior from the parent.

blocks.content: 3. Flexibility

["Realization: A class can implement multiple interfaces at the same time.
"]
items: Realization: A class can implement multiple interfaces at the same time.

blocks.content: Example: A class can be both Payable and Serializable.

["Inheritance: A class can extend only one parent class.
"]
items: Inheritance: A class can extend only one parent class.

blocks.content: Example: Dog can extend Animal, but cannot extend another class simultaneously.
4. Code Reuse

["Realization: Mainly about defining capabilities and contracts, not sharing code.
","Inheritance: Mainly about reusing existing code and common behavior.
"]
items: Realization: Mainly about defining capabilities and contracts, not sharing code.
Inheritance: Mainly about reusing existing code and common behavior.

blocks.content: 5. Dependency

["Realization: The class depends only on the interface contract, making it easier to replace implementations.
","Inheritance: The child depends heavily on the parent's structure and behavior.
"]
items: Realization: The class depends only on the interface contract, making it easier to replace implementations.
Inheritance: The child depends heavily on the parent's structure and behavior.

blocks.content: 6. UML Notation

["Realization: Dashed line pointing to an interface.
","Inheritance: Solid line pointing to a parent class."]
items: Realization: Dashed line pointing to an interface.
Inheritance: Solid line pointing to a parent class.

blocks.content: 6. Realization in UML

In UML class diagrams, realization is shown as a dashed line with an open hollow arrowhead pointing from the implementing class to the interface. The interface is usually drawn with the stereotype «interface» above its name.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781423478576-156616636.png
Each class has its own fields and its own implementation ofsend()andisAvailable().
But all three realize the sameNotificationChannelcontract they're interchangeable wherever that interface is used.
7. Why Realization Matters
Realization is not just a technical mechanism. It's a design decision that unlocks three powerful capabilities:
1. Code that works with anything
Any code that depends on an interface automatically works with every class that realizes it present and future. You write it once, it works with all implementations.
2. Open-Closed Principle
Adding a new implementation (e.g. WhatsAppChannel) requires zero changes to existing code.
You just write a new class that realizes the interface.
Everything that uses NotificationChannel instantly works with it. This is "open for extension, closed for modification."
3. Testability through mock implementations
In tests, you create a simple "fake" implementation of the interface. No real email, no real SMS. Tests run in milliseconds with predictable, controllable behaviour.
8. Abstract Classes vs Interfaces
Abstract classes also require subclasses to provide implementations for abstract methods so they look similar to interfaces. The difference matters.
1. Has State (Fields)?

["Interface: Cannot store instance data. It mainly defines behavior (methods). Only constants are allowed.
","Abstract Class: Can have instance variables and maintain shared state that child classes inherit.
"]
items: Interface: Cannot store instance data. It mainly defines behavior (methods). Only constants are allowed.
Abstract Class: Can have instance variables and maintain shared state that child classes inherit.

blocks.content: 2. Has Concrete Methods?

["Interface: Mostly declares methods. (Java 8+ allows default methods with implementation.)
","Abstract Class: Can contain fully implemented methods as well as abstract methods.
"]
items: Interface: Mostly declares methods. (Java 8+ allows default methods with implementation.)
Abstract Class: Can contain fully implemented methods as well as abstract methods.

blocks.content: 3. Multiple Inheritance?

["Interface: A class can implement multiple interfaces.
","Abstract Class: A class can extend only one abstract class.
"]
items: Interface: A class can implement multiple interfaces.
Abstract Class: A class can extend only one abstract class.

blocks.content: 4. Constructor?

["Interface: Cannot have constructors because interfaces cannot be instantiated.
","Abstract Class: Can have constructors that initialize common data for child classes.
"]
items: Interface: Cannot have constructors because interfaces cannot be instantiated.
Abstract Class: Can have constructors that initialize common data for child classes.

blocks.content: 5. When to Use?

["Interface: Use when you want to define a common capability or contract that many unrelated classes can follow.
"]
items: Interface: Use when you want to define a common capability or contract that many unrelated classes can follow.

blocks.content: Example: Payable, Sortable, Runnable.

["Abstract Class: Use when related classes share common code, fields, and behavior.
"]
items: Abstract Class: Use when related classes share common code, fields, and behavior.

blocks.content: Example: Animal, Vehicle, Employee.
6. Relationship Type
Interface: Represents a "Can Do" relationship.
Example:
["Bird can fly","Robot can fly"]
items: Bird can fly
Robot can fly

blocks.content: Both can implement Flyable even though they are unrelated.
Abstract Class: Represents an "Is A" relationship.
Example:
["Dog is an Animal","Cat is an Animal"]
items: Dog is an Animal
Cat is an Animal

blocks.content: They share common characteristics inherited from Animal.

ANALOGY: INTERFACE: A DRIVING LICENCE. ABSTRACT CLASS: A VEHICLE MANUAL.

A driving licence says "this person can operate a vehicle" it defines the capability. Any person from any background can get one; it's a cross-cutting certification. That's an interface. 

A vehicle manual is specific to one vehicle family it contains shared procedures and parts for all variants of that model. That's an abstract class shared implementation for a related group.

blocks.content: 9. Real-World Patterns Built on Realization
Realization is the backbone of several key design patterns. Recognising it makes these patterns much easier to understand.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1781423478729-726360371.png
10. Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Partial implementation (missing methods)
If a class claims to implement an interface but doesn't provide all the methods, the compiler rejects it. The contract must be fully honoured there is no partial realization.
MISSING METHOD: WON'T COMPILE
ALL METHODS IMPLEMENTED
Mistake 2: Fat interfaces (too many methods)
An interface with 20 methods forces every implementing class to provide 20 methods even if it only cares about 3. This violates the Interface Segregation Principle. Keep interfaces small and focused.
FAT INTERFACE: CLASSES ARE FORCED TO IMPLEMENT IRRELEVANT METHODS
SEGREGATED INTERFACES: EACH CLASS IMPLEMENTS ONLY WHAT IT NEEDS
Mistake 3: Confusing realization with inheritance in UML

In diagrams, using a solid arrow (inheritance) when you mean a dashed arrow (realization), or vice versa, gives a completely wrong picture of your design. Remember: dashed = implements interface. Solid = extends class.
11. Summary

The interface says what; the class provides how.","In Java, realization is expressed with the implements keyword. Inheritance = solid line with open hollow arrowhead (pointing to the parent class).","Multiple classes can realize the same interface they're interchangeable wherever that interface type is used. This is \"programming to an interface.\"","Realization enables: extensibility (add new classes without changing callers), testability (fake implementations for tests), and loose coupling.","Use an interface when defining a capability multiple unrelated classes can fulfil. Use an abstract class when sharing code and state among closely related classes.","Keep interfaces small (Interface Segregation Principle) each should define one focused capability. Fat interfaces force unnecessary implementations.","Realization is the foundation of Strategy, Observer, Command, Factory, Decorator, and Repository patterns."]
items: Realization is the relationship where a class fulfils the contract defined by an interface. The interface says what; the class provides how.
In Java, realization is expressed with the implements keyword. The class must provide concrete code for every method in the interface.
A class can realize multiple interfaces simultaneously unlike inheritance, where a class can only extend one parent.
In UML: realization = dashed line with open hollow arrowhead (pointing to the interface). Inheritance = solid line with open hollow arrowhead (pointing to the parent class).
Multiple classes can realize the same interface they're interchangeable wherever that interface type is used. This is "programming to an interface."
Realization enables: extensibility (add new classes without changing callers), testability (fake implementations for tests), and loose coupling.
Use an interface when defining a capability multiple unrelated classes can fulfil. Use an abstract class when sharing code and state among closely related classes.
Keep interfaces small (Interface Segregation Principle) each should define one focused capability. Fat interfaces force unnecessary implementations.
Realization is the foundation of Strategy, Observer, Command, Factory, Decorator, and Repository patterns.
